Restatement: Refine the 12‑month linehaul efficiency plan (no new services or network redesign) to cut cost‑per‑mile and protect share in East–Central and Central–South by focusing on routing/scheduling, asset utilization, fuel surcharge controls, and short‑term commercial actions under sparse data.  
Actions (step‑by‑step): 1) Run 8‑week route‑rationalization sprints on top 6 trunk lanes: map current stops, simulate re‑sequences, pilot new schedules with one dispatcher team in week 2, iterate weekly; 2) Trial dynamic shoulder routing to fold low‑density moves into existing trunks (4‑week trial, monitored daily); 3) Set lane load‑factor targets and publish weekly scorecards to dispatch with a simple incentive for hits/misses (start reporting week 1); 4) Centralize fuel surcharge governance, connect pump‑price feed, and update surcharge monthly; 5) Use a short contract playbook to offer selective, time‑boxed 5% discounts in at‑risk corridors while tightening delivery windows/penalties (legal template ready in week 2); 6) Enforce idle‑reduction and driver pairing SOPs to increase trailer turns (checklist + dispatcher signoff).  
Expected impact and key assumptions: 1) route sprints → 3–7% cost/mile reduction (assumes re‑sequencing is SLA‑compatible and data for top lanes is reliable); 2) shoulder routing → 1–3% cost/mile and marginal reliability improvement (assumes capacity on trunks); 3) load‑factor scorecards → 2–5% cost/mile and steadier utilization (assumes dispatcher adoption and modest schedule flexibility); 4) surcharge tuning → offsets ~50% of fuel volatility impact (assumes customers accept monthly adjustment); 5) selective discounting → preserves volumes with controlled margin loss (assumes contractual levers and monitoring); 6) idle reduction → 1–2% cost/mile and faster turns (assumes driver cooperation).  
Priorities (top 3–5): Highest priority = 1) route‑rationalization sprints, 3) load‑factor targets/scorecards, and 4) centralized fuel surcharge tuning, because they deliver the largest, fastest cost/mile impact, are executable within weeks, and directly counter fuel pressure and competitor pricing; next priority = 5) selective corridor discounts to defend at‑risk volumes.  
Implementation risks & mitigations: data gaps risking poor changes—mitigate with conservative pilots, weekly manual KPI reconciliations, and limiting changes to top lanes; customer resistance to schedule/price changes—mitigate via targeted communications and short trial offers; dispatcher/driver noncompliance—mitigate with brief training, checklists, and short‑term incentives; fuel spikes—mitigate with rapid surcharge updates and review of a limited hedging policy.

Restatement: Convert the four prioritized linehaul initiatives (route‑rationalization sprints, load‑factor scorecards, centralized fuel‑surcharge tuning, selective corridor discounts + idle‑reduction SOPs) into a sequenced 12‑month execution roadmap that meets a minimum 3% average cost‑per‑mile reduction while keeping incremental cash spend <= $1.2M and avoiding heavy up‑front tool purchases.  
Actions (12‑month roadmap, step‑by‑step with spend vs process): 1) Q1 (weeks 0–12) — Launch 8‑week route‑rationalization pilots on top 6 trunks: map lanes, run re‑sequence simulations, pilot new schedules with one dispatcher team, collect daily KPI; (pilot = primarily process, modest analytics support spend). 2) Q1–Q2 — Implement load‑factor weekly scorecards and short dispatcher incentives: define targets, build simple dashboard, start 12‑week incentive pilot; (process + small incentive pool). 3) Q1 onward — Centralize fuel surcharge governance: connect pump‑price feed to a monthly update cadence and issue customer communications; (process/tooling minimal). 4) Q2–Q3 — Pilot selective 5% time‑boxed discounts in at‑risk East–Central/Central–South lanes with tightened windows/penalties and legal playbook; (commercial action, negligible tooling spend). 5) Q2–Q4 — Roll out idle‑reduction/drivers‑pairing SOPs and dispatcher signoff checklists, then scale best practices based on pilot results; (process change, training cost). 6) Q3 (conditional) — If pilots justify, invest in modest analytics/telematics integration for broader automation (defer to avoid front‑loading spend).  
Expected impact, rough spend and key assumptions (per action): 1) Route sprints → ~1.4–2.0% cost/mi contribution; pilot spend ~$120k (analytics support/man‑hours); assumes top lanes have re‑sequence flexibility and SLAs are respected. 2) Load‑factor scorecards → ~0.8–1.2% contribution; dashboard + incentive pilot ~$120k total; assumes dispatcher adoption and minor schedule elasticity. 3) Fuel‑surcharge tuning → ~0.2–0.4% net effect on effective cost/mile (stabilizes margin vs spikes); tooling <$15k; assumes customers accept monthly adjustments. 4) Selective discounts → protects volumes with limited margin drag (net neutral to slightly negative on cost/mile); legal/template/time ~$10k; assumes competitor pressure persists in targeted corridors. 5) Idle‑reduction SOPs → ~0.2–0.4% contribution; training/rollout ~$25k; assumes driver cooperation. 6) Deferred telematics/analytics integration → potential incremental upside 0.5–1.0% but estimated $500–700k spend and therefore recommended only after pilots validate ROI. Planned 12‑month incremental spend (pilots + tooling + incentives + training) ≈ $505k; H1 planned spend ≈ $260k — both comfortably under the $1.2M cap and avoid front‑loading.  
Recommendation to drop/shrink: Defer and substantially shrink any company‑wide telematics purchase this year (recommended to delay $500–700k spend until post‑pilot go/no‑go); limit incentive pools to pilot scale (~$120k) and only scale if ROI meets pre‑defined thresholds.  
Implementation risks & mitigations (cost‑target and budget focus): Risk — low adoption or poor data yields <3% savings; Mitigate — conservative 8‑week pilots with stop/go gates and weekly KPI review, require pre‑set thresholds for scaling; Risk — budget overrun from analytics buy; Mitigate — hard stop on telematics procurement until Q3 review and reserve a $200k contingency within the $1.2M cap; Risk — customer pushback on surcharge/slots; Mitigate — staged customer communications and short trial offers with clear end dates.

Actions (step‑by‑step): 1) Stand up a 30‑minute weekly Linehaul Ops review (Linehaul Manager lead) to review exceptions and take actions; 2) Build a lane‑level dashboard in our existing BI tool (Ops analyst to create templates, automated daily/weekly pulls where available); 3) Assign clear owners for each KPI/initiative (Dispatch Lead for load/utilization, Fleet Lead for turns/idle, Commercial Lead for surcharge/discounts, Finance Controller for cost/spend); 4) Run 2‑week tactical pilot huddles (dispatcher + pilot lead) and a monthly Steering Committee (COO + Finance) to review pilots and approve scale; 5) Predefine corrective playbooks (reschedule, re‑sequence, temporary commercial holdback, or hotspot dispatch surge) and stop/go gates for pilots; 6) Implement automated alerts for threshold breaches and a weekly manual reconciliation for sparse data.  
Expected impact & key assumptions (by action): 1) Weekly reviews shorten detection lag and increase corrective velocity (improves chance of hitting ≥3%; assumes timely data feeds); 2) Dashboard cuts analysis time and improves decision reliability (assumes BI can access lane data with minor ETL); 3) Named owners raise accountability and execution speed (assumes role bandwidth and mandate); 4) Frequent huddles accelerate iteration and limit costly scale‑ups (assumes attendance and decision authority); 5) Playbooks reduce time‑to‑remediate and cap cost creep (assumes playbooks pre‑approved by legal/commercial); 6) Alerts + manual checks mitigate data gaps and prevent blind spots (assumes one dedicated analyst or deputized person).  
KPIs (6–8) with owner & cadence: 1) Cost per mile (lane) — Finance Controller — weekly; 2) Load factor % (lane) — Dispatch Lead — weekly; 3) On‑time performance (trunk) — Ops Manager — daily summary, weekly review; 4) Fuel spend vs budget (linehaul) — Finance Controller — weekly; 5) Trailer turns per unit — Fleet Lead — weekly; 6) # lanes > deviation threshold — Linehaul Manager — weekly; 7) Incentive attainment % (pilot) — HR/Dispatch — weekly; 8) Pilot ROI vs target — Finance/Linehaul — monthly.  
Implementation risks, mitigations & escalation path: Risk = slow detection/data gaps → mitigate with automated alerts + weekly manual reconciliations and (recommended tweak) a 0.1–0.2 FTE temporary data analyst for 3–6 months (flagged for approval); Risk = weak follow‑through → mitigate with named owners, decision authority at cadences, and short incentive levers; Escalation: if a lane’s cost/mi misses glidepath by >5% for 2 consecutive weeks, Dispatch Lead executes playbook within 48 hours and notifies Linehaul Manager; if unresolved after 7 days or if spend variance >10% of pilot allocation, escalate to COO + Finance for urgent pause/redirect decision.
